public_summary: TESS shows a steady 1100 ppm dip every 11.4 days lasting 1.7 hours on a quiet K-dwarf, with no odd/even difference or nearby star that could mimic it and a planet-sized depth. The short duration fits the star if the planet is grazing the star, which is allowed. The signal looks like a grazing super-Earth/mini-Neptune; leftover tiny secondary signal and large starspots make follow-up photometry and radial velocities needed to rule out a diluted binary completely.

observing.headline: Tessa found a possible 2.7 Earth-radius planet that dips 1103 ppm for 3.1 hours every 11.42872 days around K dwarf TIC 61220826 (Tmag 10.7, 4324 K, 78 pc away).

observing.telescope: A 1 m telescope can catch one transit with per-transit SNR 5.8 and a 2 m telescope can with SNR 10.1, while a 0.4 m telescope at SNR 2.7 cannot see the 1103 ppm dip in one transit and would need many transits stacked or a space telescope.
observing.refuted_if: Tessa is wrong if data good enough to see the 1103 ppm dip, such as 1 m data with SNR 5.8 or 2 m data with SNR 10.1, shows no dip within 23.8 min of the predicted time from the 11.42872-day period, or if the dip has a different depth in different colours, which means a blended binary.
observing.confirmed_by: It would be confirmed as a planet if the 1103 ppm transits repeat on the 11.42872-day period within the timing errors of 25.8 min to 32.6 min and radial velocities give a mass consistent with the 2.7 Earth-radius size.
